audits.mathematicalReason: Relabeling the positive dimensions if necessary, take XY=24, XZ=48, and YZ=72. Then X²=(24·48)/72=16, so X=4, Y=6, and Z=12. Their sum is 22 units. The alternative volume route is valid: (XYZ)²=24·48·72, giving volume 288, and division by the respective face areas recovers the same dimensions. Positivity selects the positive square roots.

Write a_n=2^(b_n/19). Then b_0=0, b_1=1, and b_n=b_(n−1)+2b_(n−2), giving b_n=(2^n−(−1)^n)/3. Thus S_k=Σb_n=(2^(k+2)−3−(−1)^k)/6. Unique prime factorization shows that 2^(S_k/19) is an integer exactly when 19 divides S_k. For even k this requires 2^k≡1 mod 19; for odd k it requires 2^(k+1)≡1 mod 19. The order of 2 modulo 19 is 18: 2^9≡−1 and 2^6≡7 rule out every proper divisor of 18. The first qualifying k is therefore 17. Direct recurrence iteration modulo 19 is also a valid route.

Since xy=−2, both denominators are nonzero. The expression factors as (x²+y²)(x³+y³)/(x²y²). Here x²+y²=(x+y)²−2xy=20 and x³+y³=(x+y)((x+y)²−3xy)=88, while x²y²=4. The value is therefore 20·88/4=440. Alternatively, x and y satisfy t²=4t+2, so their power sums obey p_n=4p_(n−1)+2p_(n−2); this gives p_5=1744 and the equivalent evaluation 4+p_5/4=440.

An unsuccessful two-toss round has probability (2/3)(3/5)=2/5 by independence. Amelia's winning probability is therefore Σ[(2/5)^j/3], for j≥0, which converges to (1/3)/(1−2/5)=5/9. Equivalently, the reset recurrence is W=1/3+(2/5)W. The probability of surviving N complete rounds is (2/5)^N→0, so there is no nontermination probability. Thus p=5, q=9, and q−p=4.

The fixed factors already give four distinct roots: 1±i and 2±2i. Both roots of the middle quadratic must therefore belong to this set, with multiplicity allowed, and their product must be 4. The only admissible pairs are (1+i,2−2i) and (1−i,2+2i); repeated-root possibilities do not have product 4. Their sums give c=3−i or 3+i, hence |c|=√10. Substituting any shared root into c=r+4/r gives the same possibilities, and its companion root is indeed among the four existing roots.

By independence, the probability of a tie in bin k is 2^(−k)·2^(−k)=4^(−k). Summing the disjoint tie events gives P(tie)=(1/4)/(1−1/4)=1/3, with convergence justified by ratio 1/4. Exchanging the red and green balls preserves the distribution, so the two strict orderings have equal probabilities. Each is (1−1/3)/2=1/3.

routes.label: Enumerate integer points and chord lengths

audits.mathematicalReason: Every integer point on x²+y²=25 has x+y odd. Hence the squared distance between two such points is a positive even integer, so RS²≥2. The diameter bounds PQ²≤100; because PQ is irrational, PQ²≠100, and evenness sharpens the bound to PQ²≤98. Thus PQ/RS≤√(98/2)=7. This is attained by four distinct points P=(3,4), Q=(−4,−3), R=(4,−3), S=(3,−4), for which PQ=7√2 and RS=√2. Enumeration of the twelve integer points provides another valid way to establish these extrema.

Every allowed transformation fixes the origin. A composition returning T must also fix its two other vertices individually because their distances from the origin are different, so the composition must be the identity. An identity triple contains zero or two reflections. With zero reflections, the quarter-turn exponents are permutations of (1,1,2) or (2,3,3), giving 6 sequences. With two reflections, they must be the two different axis reflections, and the rotation must be 180°; all 3!=6 orders work because the half-turn commutes with both reflections. The total is 12. Counting partial composition states is also a valid alternative.
